newsitem.title: USA: ABC to unveil 24-hour online news service.
newsitem.headline: ABC to unveil 24-hour online news service.

text.p: Walt Disney Co's ABC News division said it will unveil Thursday its foray into the Internet news arena with ABC.news.com, a 24-hour online news service squarely aimed at competing with MSNBC, the joint venture of NBC and Microsoft Corp.

Last month, ABC formed a few formidable partnerships as part of this move, including a deal with America Online Inc, Netscape Communications Corp and invested $100 million in Starwave Corp, acquiring a third of the firm which runs popular sites such as Mr. Showbiz and NBA.com.
The service will be free and supported by advertising.
Analysts said that while ABC News is behind MSNBC, which was launched by Microsoft and NBC last July, ABC can learn from some of the trials of competing online news services.

"It's a bit late, but in the Internet business, there is no such thing as too late when you have a big brand," said Gary Arlen, president of Arlen Communications in Bethesda, Md. "And to someone who just discovered cyberspace on Friday, they won't know ABC just started and MSNBC and CNN have been there," Arlen added. CNN also has a 24-hour online news site.

So far, some Internet-based publishing ventures have been losing money and some have folded. Time Warner Inc's Pathfinder site has had several executive shuffles and it is believed to be losing money. ABC exited a Web-based venture with the Washington Post Co called Politics Now.
Disney executives said last month that they do not expect to make money from the ABCnews.com until the year 2000.

But its partnerships could guarantee some large numbers of viewers. With AOL, ABC plans a cross-marketing relationship, so that AOL members will have their own customized version of ABCnews.com, available only to the eight million AOL members.

And Starwave, ABC's joint venture partner, runs one of the most heavily trafficked Web sites on the Internet, with its ESPNet Sportszone online sports service. Starwave, which is privately held in Bellevue, Wash., was founded by Paul Allen, co-founder with Bill Gates of Microsoft.

"Well-funded ventures are starting to turn a profit," said Rob Kuckro, editor of the Information and Interactive Services Report. He also sited Softbank's ZDNet news service and CNET as successful Internet-based news ventures. CNET, a television show and an online news service on computing, is still losing money but reaping more revenues from the Internet.
